hero.title_html: Infrastructure that won’t wake you up at 3 a.m.
hero.lead: I design, automate and run the environments your product lives on — from the first Dockerfile to production monitoring. I also write the code that ties it all together.

services.title: What I do
services.intro: Five areas, one rule: everything I build can be recreated from a repository and understood without me.

items.name: CI/CD
items.title: Pipelines you can trust
items.text: Tests, builds and deployments in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI. Every merge reaches production predictably, and a rollback is one command, not a midnight rescue mission.

items.name: Containers
items.title: Docker and Kubernetes, no magic
items.text: Minimal multi-stage images, running as non-root, scanned for vulnerabilities. Compose where it's enough, Kubernetes where it makes sense.

items.name: Infrastructure
items.title: Servers as code
items.text: VPS, AWS or Hetzner — described in Terraform and Ansible. You rebuild the environment from a repository in minutes, not from one person's memory.

items.name: Monitoring
items.title: See the problem before your customer does
items.text: Metrics, logs and alerts that actually mean something. Plus server hardening, TLS and backups — with regularly tested restores.

items.name: Development
items.title: Code that holds it together
items.text: APIs and backend services, integrations between systems, scripts and internal tools that take repetitive manual work off your team.

Concrete scope, milestones and a quote. You know what you pay for and when you get it.

principles: Docs are part of the delivery

projects.title: From manual deploys to a pipeline in six weeks
projects.summary: The app ran on a single server and was deployed by hand over FTP — usually on a Friday evening. No tested backups, no monitoring; every update was a gamble.
sections: One person knew the server. A deploy took about 40 minutes and ended with manually checking whether it “works”. Customers were the ones reporting outages.

Containerised the app (multi-stage, non-root images) and built a GitHub Actions pipeline: tests → build → Trivy scan → GHCR registry → deploy with health check and automatic rollback. Staging and production described in Terraform and Ansible. Prometheus, Grafana and chat alerts. Nightly database backups with a weekly restore test.
Deployments became a routine daytime task, and the team got documentation and runbooks to run the environment on their own.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
items: How much does setting up CI/CD or containerising an app cost?

It depends on the starting point and scope. After a short call and a review of your current setup you get a quote for a specific milestone — with a clearly defined outcome — or a rate for ongoing support. You can indicate a budget range in the form.
Yes. I work remotely with companies in Poland and abroad. Access to servers and repositories goes through accounts you can revoke at any time — nothing stays tied to me.
What infrastructure do you work with?
Linux VPS and dedicated servers (e.g. Hetzner, OVH), AWS, Docker and Docker Compose, Kubernetes, GitHub Actions and GitLab CI, Terraform and Ansible, nginx, Prometheus and Grafana.
Can you take over maintenance of existing systems?
Yes. I start by reviewing and documenting the current state, then clean things up in small, reversible steps — no downtime and no rewrite from scratch.
What do I get when the project is finished?

All configuration as code in your repository, documentation, runbooks for common incidents and a short training for your team. The infrastructure is fully yours — no dependency on a single person or vendor.
Do you also build applications, not just infrastructure?
Yes — APIs and backend services (Node.js, Python, Go), integrations between systems and internal tools. Often it is the code that ties the automation together.
